newsitem.title: Thailand: TV exit poll projects dead heat in Thai election.
newsitem.headline: TV exit poll projects dead heat in Thai election.

text.p: A television exit poll broadcast after voting in Thailand's elections closed on Sunday projected a dead heat between the Democrat Party and the New Aspiration Party (NAP) with 124 seats each.
Channel 9 television reported that the Chart Pattana party would win 52 while the incumbent Chart Thai party would secure 35 seats in the 393-seat lower house of parliament.

Analysts said that the exit poll was probably conducted on a small sample of voters and might not be very accurate. Some unofficial results were expected to start trickling in soon after the polls closed at 0800 GMT.
The exit poll also showed the Social Action Party taking 19 seats and five other smaller parties winning the rest.
Opinion polls taken before voting closed had shown the Democrats, led by former premier Chuan Leekpai, and the NAP headed by outgoing Defence Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh running neck and neck.
Analysts had predicted the closest race ever. No previous Thai election has resulted in a tie between the two top parties.
A day of brisk voting across the country was marred by a shooting and reports of bribery and intimidation.
A guman shot and seriously wounded a policeman, an election official and a voter in the western Bangkok suburb of Bang Khae, but was arrested shortly after, police said.
Television stations reported that some voters had complained in the northern province of Petchabun that they had received marked ballot papers at polling booths in the area.
Election supervisors were investigating the allegations.
Pollwatch, the election watchdog, estimated that politicians had spent between 20 billion and 30 billion baht ($800 million and $1.2 billion) to date on vote-buying.
Most of the vote-buying was conducted in the northeast, the poorest region in Thailand with more than one-third of all seats being contested in the polls.
Voter turnout was reported to be high as people walked, drove and even rowed through flooded streets to cast their vote.

More than 38 million Thais were eligible to vote in the polls in which 2,310 candidates from 13 parties vied for the 393 seats in parliament. It was Thailand's fourth election in four years and the second in 16 months.
